articles.title: In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026
articles.summary: And yes, doomsday falls on Friday the 13th.
articles.body:
In exactly a month, on November 13, 2026, the world will end. Fittingly, our impending apocalypse falls on Friday the 13th .

At least, that was the prediction made by University of Illinois physicist Heinz von Foerster in a highly cited Science paper published in 1960. Though talks of supposed doomsday have renewed in recent months thanks to hyperbolic anxieties over runaway, sentient artificial intelligence, von Foerster had a much different calamity in mind.

For more than a century, the prevailing fear, dating back to English economist Thomas Malthus who lived between 1766 to 1834, was of a booming population outrunning its food supply. Famine would ensue. But Von Foerster broke from that view. He assumed (correctly, as it turns out) that human ingenuity would keep the world mostly fed. The problem, he argued, was that the population would keep accelerating, toward "infinity."

In a now infamous quote, von Foerster predicted, "Our great—great—grandchildren will not starve to death," von Foerster and his co-authors wrote. "They will be squeezed to death." Homo sapiens' last gasping breath, they predicted, would peter out in the fall of 2026.

It's pretty clear that von Foerster's estimate was dead wrong. Not only is the global population ( around 8.3 billion people ) not expanding near the rate it was when he was writing, but there are actually concerns it's moving in the opposite direction . In dozens of countries around the world, from South Korea and Japan to much of Western Europe, the concern among demographers has shifted from worries about overpopulation to declining birth rates.

In the United States, President Donald Trump has jumped on the issue, calling himself the " fertilization president " offering tax incentives for new families and even exploring medals for women who give birth to six or more children. Joseph Stalin previously championed that last idea.

So how was a prediction so wrong and still so influential? Human population experts speaking with Popular Science say von Foerster and his contemporaries based their prediction on real trends from the past while utterly failing to see the world changing right before their eyes. Though they may have accurately measured growth rates up to that point, that only tells part of the story.

"He got the picture right just as that picture ceased to be right," Rockefeller University and Columbia University professor and mathematical biologist Joel Cohen tells Popular Science. Cohen has studied human population changes for years and published the influential 1995 book How Many People Can the Earth Support?

"Von Foerster didn't know at the time, and in fact, nobody knew" that the all-time population growth had already happened, Cohen adds. "The all-time peak happened in the early 1960s."

Why did experts think the world would end on Friday the 13th?

Von Foerster and his colleagues published their "Doomsday" paper on November 4, 1960. The dramatic pronouncement hinges on an equation that projects the human population into the future based on past trends.

The team gathered 24 estimates of world population dating back 2,000 years. The key assumption underpinning their logic was that humans differ from other animals because of our unique ability to cooperate and innovate.

Fruit flies in a jar eventually level off as crowding and competition take their toll. Humans, on the other hand, the authors argue, work the other way. The more of us there are, the better we get at cooperating. And the better we get at cooperation, the faster our population grows.

Follow that curve forward, and the population doesn't just grow; it rockets toward infinity, hitting the so-called mathematical wall on November 13, 2026, give or take five years.

Von Foerster wasn't alone in sounding the alarm either. Eight years later, biologist Paul R. Ehrlich would publish The Population Bomb , arguably the most influential single text fueling overpopulation fears.

"Both of those guys were right looking backward, but wrong looking forward," Cohen says.

At a glance, thinking the future will resemble the past seems pretty reasonable. The human population grew steadily but slowly over much of our roughly 300,000 years of humanity. But that changed radically with the onset of globalization, colonization, and the Industrial Revolution.

How fast is the human population growing?

As Darrell Bricker and John Ibbitson note in their 2020 book Empty Planet: The Shock of Global Population Decline , human population passed the one billion mark somewhere around 1800. That doubled to two billion by 1927. Then doubled again just less than 50 years later in 1974. It would then only take another 13 years to cross the five billion mark. And in 2022, we surpassed eight billion.

That remarkable explosion had many causes, Cohen says, but among the most important was the spread of cheap, calorie-dense crops like potatoes and corn from the Americas.

Crucially, though, humans weren't necessarily having way more kids. They were just far better at keeping them alive.

Human population booms weren't because people were having more kids

"Humanity got better at keeping the people who were born alive through simple, but important innovations like the germ theory of disease, sanitation, nutrition," University of Texas Associate professor and economic demographer Dean Spears tells Popular Science.

Demographers like Spears study human populations and how they change over time. He published a book on the topic titled After the Spike , earlier this year. Advances in nutrition and medicine "caused early life mortality rates to fall, so more of the humans who were born survived and that caused the population to grow."

Factoring in longer life expectancy and reductions in child mortality around the world blows a huge hole in Von Foerster's calculations. Death rates can only fall so far, and once most children survive, families tend to have fewer of them.

The population boom was a one time explosion, not an ever-accelerating loop.

Overpopulation fears are actually based on a misunderstanding

Von Foerster's assumption of endlessly accelerating growth, Spears says, was "based on a misunderstanding of where population growth comes from."

Experts specializing in human population studies at the time actually knew that was the case, Spears notes.

Neither von Foerster's nor Ehrlich (who wrote The Population Bomb) were human population experts. Von Foerster's background was in physics and philosophy. Ehrlich was a biologist. But they were both great at getting attention.

Indeed, academics at the time reportedly sent flustered letters to the editor at Science , calling the prediction "ridiculous" and "manifestly absurd."

"There was never, even at that time, any reason to think that it would keep growing fast like that." Spears says. "Paul Ehrlich was a biologist who studied butterflies , not human demography."

Why people are worried about declining birth rates now

In the later 20th century, population growth actually started declining quite rapidly thanks to a convergence of a variety of factors.

The "Green Revolution" in farming meant that more food could be grown on the same plot of land, which extinguished fears of humanity suddenly starving itself. The first birth control pill , approved by the Federal Drug Administration (FDA) in the U.S. in 1957 , also gave women more autonomy to decide when and how many children to have.

These trends, along with global population shifts away from rural areas and towards more urban areas, would eventually shift concerns away from overpopulation and towards declining birth rates.

Although demographers and policy experts debate how much people should worry about declining birth rates, it is generally agreed that an older population that significantly outnumbers younger people can lead to long-term strains on the country's economy and social services.

With fewer workers needed in the field, more and more people moved to cities. Historically, families living on farms or agricultural communities tend to have more children than those in urban areas because those children could work the land and, in a purely economic sense, provide more labor and, hopefully, make the family more money. In more urban areas, another child meant another mouth to feed rather than an extra pair of hands.

In the later part of the 20th century, women in many parts of the world gained far more autonomy through education, work, and access to contraception, which demographers agree is among the biggest drivers of demographic change over the past half century.

Some governments went further. China's one-child policy ( introduced in 1979 ) and India's forced sterilization campaigns ( between 1975-1977 ) were heavy-handed responses fuelled by overpopulation panic. What makes those coercive policies all the more tragic, Spears notes, is that birth rates likely would have fallen without them.

"What we're seeing now, a world of low and falling birth rates, is actually nothing new, but just the latest moment in a decades-long or longer trajectory of falling global birth rates on average happening essentially everywhere," Sears says.

"I would say that the coercive [state-sanctioned] school [of thought] was counterproductive," Cohen adds. He went on to say he believes similar government-led initiatives encouraging families to have more children today, like the Trump administration's proposed baby medal, are "counterproductive." Real, meaningful generational changes in population, Cohen notes, are more often the product of society-level macro trends beyond the scope of any one politician or party.

Today, about a month shy of von Foerster's doomsday, around 55 percent of the world's countries , home to more than two-thirds of its people, have fertility rates below replacement level . That's the rate (about 2.1 children per woman) demographers use to denote where a population replaces itself from one generation to the next.

In other words, not only is the human population not hurtling towards infinity, but in much of the world, it's actually on track to eventually shrink. Experts largely agree birth rates are falling. Whether that's a problem to be solved is less clear-cut.

At the family level, having fewer children can mean more money, resources, and personal attention invested in each one. It can also mean more independence, opportunity, and choice for those who decided parenthood just isn't for them.

At the broader economic or societal level, though, Spears argues there are good reasons to want birth rates to stabilize rather than keep falling. Pay-as-you-go social programs like Social Security depend on young workers to fund older people's retirements. Fewer people also means fewer shared resources and services for everyone else.

"If you want to go out and eat lunch at a taco truck, but you're the only person nearby who wants it, then the taco truck's not going to be there," Spears says. "And if you're a school child wanting to go to school, there might not be enough other children for there to be a classroom nearby that's suitable for you."

Those are legitimate concerns, though Cohen warns that focusing too much on abstract numbers and trends can blur a more immediate issue directly in front of us. Globally, children are still regularly going underfed, so much so that the World Health Organization estimates around 22 percent of children under the age of five experience stunted growth from malnutrition.

"We are doing so poorly by the children we have that I can't understand why the emphasis is on making more children," Cohen says. "We're talking about having more children when we don't take care of the children we have. What the heck is that?"

But even for those who do worry about falling birth rates, Spears cautions against politicians promising quick fixes. This isn't a short-term emergency, he says, but a "generational challenge." One thing is clear though: Neither Spears nor Cohen are losing sleep over von Foerster's November 13 death date.

"I'm sure not acting as if I'm too concerned about it," Cohen says. "I'm still paying my bills. I'm still paying my taxes."

articles.title: Shane Gillis joked about women's gym shorts. Women are turning the insult around.
articles.summary: Women are pushing back against Shane Gillis's jokes about women's gym clothes on SNL, using humor, workout videos and pointed criticism to call out misogyny,...
articles.body:
Shane Gillis opened his Saturday Night Live monologue by announcing he's going back to the gym because he needs to lose weight. But the self-deprecation quickly turned outward.

"I haven't been to the gym in so long, I didn't know women just dress like whores now," Gillis said during his Oct. 10 appearance on the show as host. "Look, I'm sorry, there's no other way to describe it," he continued, describing women's brightly colored, tight-fitting workout shorts as "artificial bait."

"And don't look, you're not allowed to look," he added, joking that he was likely captured gawking in the background of their TikToks.

In another bit, the 38-year-old described an encounter with a "beautiful woman" while hiking and his attempt to appear nonthreatening as they approached each other on an otherwise empty trail. "I gotta figure out what face to make to let her know that I'm not here to…" Gillis said, trailing off. "Which is a tough face to make, I don't know if you've ever made that face."

The comments quickly drew backlash on social media. Actor Dan Levy was among those who criticized Gillis and argued that degrading women for wearing shorts to the gym was misogynistic. Levy also urged more men to speak up when women are objectified.

But it's not just word choice, according to content creator Brenna Perez . In an Instagram video , she highlighted the contradiction between Gillis's hiking story and his comments about women at the gym. In one scenario, the comedian appeared to understand why a woman might be uncomfortable around an unfamiliar man, she said. In the next, he suggested that women's choice of workout apparel was inviting men's attention.

The latter, she said, reinforces a familiar attitude used to blame women for unwanted sexual attention: that their clothing means they were somehow asking for it.

"People are not being overly sensitive or unfunny by pointing out that this is very much a part of the problem," said Perez.

Some women are also responding on TikTok, posting videos of themselves working out in the very shorts Gillis took issue with. "Just a girl in her wh*re shorts at the gym," wrote Maggie B . "Yeah Shane Gillis, I wear shorts to the gym. Don't look or you might see a baddie lifting heavier than you!" wrote another creator, who goes by Singlemamadrama, over a clip of herself lifting. Anyeé, who says she's a wellness bodybuilder, shared a message for Gillis on TikTok. "Let me be clear: my outfit isn't for you, your comfort or your monologue. I train hard, I lift heavy and I'll wear whatever I want while doing it," she wrote in the caption of a video of herself doing pull-ups.

Paige Connell , a motherhood advocate and cohost of Just Us Girls podcast, pointed out what she saw as a double standard : Men wear short shorts and barely there tank tops to work out. So why is women's clothing being treated as an invitation for sexual attention?

There's also the issue of timing. Gillis's monologue aired as a sexual assault case involving seven members of a Cornell fraternity has dominated headlines and prompted a national conversation over sexual violence. A lawsuit filed by a former student, identified as Jane Doe, alleges that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple men at a fraternity house in 2024.

The case has raised questions about male accountability and the language men use while discussing women. Gillis's choice of words bears a resemblance to something Jane Doe herself said about the alleged assault during a 2025 disciplinary hearing: "I felt like bait."

Feminist writer Jessica Valenti drew a connection between the monologue and the Cornell allegations in an Instagram video , arguing that Gillis's remarks shouldn't be dismissed as simply a poorly timed joke.

"Shane Gillis knows that there is a major national conversation happening right now about sexual assault. He is very well aware of that fact. He is very well aware that tens of thousands of women — hundreds of thousands, maybe more — are sharing their stories of being raped, are talking about how painful it was when the good men in their life didn't do anything or blamed them," said Valenti. "When you demean and denigrate and dehumanize women and say that they're not real human beings, they're just whores, their clothes are bait. What do you think rape culture is?"

She also criticized SNL for giving the material a national platform. (NBC representatives for the show didn't immediately respond to Yahoo's request for comment.)

Of course, provocative comedy is hardly new territory for Gillis.

The comedian was famously dropped from the SNL cast in 2019 , just days after being hired, when past racist and homophobic remarks resurfaced. Still, he went on to have a successful career in stand-up, podcasting and television. His popularity has endured despite criticism of his material, with fans embracing his willingness to push boundaries.

In 2024, he was invited to host the very show that fired him years prior, with Saturday marking his third time returning to the SNL stage.

Gillis hasn't publicly addressed the criticism of his monologue, but he did offer an apology during the live show for accidentally dropping the F-bomb during a sketch. The word is subject to FCC broadcast restrictions. "Whore" isn't.

articles.title: In 1972, three siblings gave Washington 590 acres on Squak Mountain instead of developing it; the land became the foundation of a state park
articles.summary: On 17 June 1972, Ashley Ann Bullitt, Scott Bullitt and Jill Hamilton Bullitt transferred 590 acres of family land on Squak Mountain to Washington state
articles.body: On 17 June 1972, Ashley Ann Bullitt, Scott Bullitt and Jill Hamilton Bullitt transferred 590 acres of family land on Squak Mountain to Washington state for a wilderness park. Their gift followed decades of land purchases by their father, Stimson Bullitt, who had assembled a property of more than 600 acres and built a vacation cabin on the mountain. Rather than retain the land for private use or allow it to be developed, the siblings chose to protect it for public enjoyment under strict conditions. The donation laid the groundwork for Squak Mountain State Park, which later expanded through additional land purchases and conservation efforts. The history of the park reflects both the family’s decision and the work of local hikers, conservation advocates and public agencies that helped safeguard the surrounding foothills.How the Bullitt family acquired land on Squak MountainStimson Bullitt began acquiring property on Squak Mountain during the 1940s, gradually bringing separate parcels together into a large family holding. He came from a prominent Pacific Northwest family associated with timber and broadcasting. In 1952, he built a 2-room vacation cabin on the mountain, providing a place for his family to spend time away from the city. The property eventually covered more than 600 acres around Squak Mountain’s 2,024-foot summit. In the early 1970s, the family trust transferred the land to 3 of Bullitt’s children: Ashley Ann, Scott and Jill Hamilton Bullitt. According to the history published by Washington State Parks, their father had reportedly outlined 3 possible uses for the property: the siblings could build homes for themselves, divide the land for development or donate it for a public park. They chose the third option. On 17 June 1972, they gave 590 acres to the Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission, with conditions intended to preserve the land’s wilderness character.The decision came during a period of change around Issaquah. Construction of Interstate 90 in the 1960s contributed to suburban growth in the area, while Squak Mountain had already experienced decades of resource extraction. Coal mining became an important part of Issaquah’s economy, and logging also altered parts of the mountain. The Issaquah Alps Trails Club’s history describes the area’s mining and logging past and traces how the Bullitt gift became the foundation of the state park. The mountain lies within the traditional territory of Coast Salish Indigenous peoples. Its geological history also predates the settlement and industrial activity that later shaped the region: the underlying rocks include sediments deposited in an ancient coastal environment.The conditions that protected the original 590 acresThe Bullitt siblings did not simply donate the property for general recreation. The deed specified that the land should be managed as a wilderness park, excluding vehicles, horses, roads other than footpaths and man-made structures. Those restrictions distinguished the original donation from a conventional developed park. The family cabin did not survive for long after the land was transferred. According to the Issaquah Alps Trails Club’s account of the Bullitt family legacy, vandals had largely dismantled the 2-room building by the end of 1973. Its substantial stone fireplace remained, becoming a physical reminder of the cabin and the family’s connection to the mountain.A practical challenge remained: the donated property lacked a suitable connection to a public road for a formal trailhead and parking area. On 17 July 1984, the Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission purchased an additional 23 acres from North American Refractories Company. The land was part of the former Richmond-Harris Coal Mine property and provided access for visitors. This purchase was separate from the original Bullitt donation. The distinction matters because Squak Mountain State Park developed through several land transactions, while the wilderness conditions attached to the original 590 acres remained central to its identity.Harvey Manning and the campaign to protect the foothillsThe creation of the park was followed by a wider conservation effort to protect the mountains surrounding Issaquah. Harvey Manning, a writer and wilderness advocate, helped popularise the name “Issaquah Alps” for the local foothills. Washington State Parks recounts that Manning turned to these nearby foothills when winter snow made his usual mountain destinations difficult to reach. Manning became an influential advocate for preserving the area and was a founding member and first president of the Issaquah Alps Trails Club. He praised the Bullitt donation as “the greatest act of environmental benevolence in local history”, according to the state parks history.Bill Longwell was another important figure in the effort. A hiker, teacher and musician, he helped survey routes and organise trail-building work. Manning gave him the nickname “Chief Ranger”. The club’s own history describes Longwell as one of its original members in 1979 and credits him with extensive work improving trails on Squak and Tiger Mountains. The club’s contribution continued beyond the park’s establishment. Its volunteers have helped maintain trails, remove invasive plants and support restoration work with Washington State Parks. Its 2025 account of Squak Mountain also records the organisation’s first group hike, led by Longwell on 6 June 1979.Later land acquisitions expanded the parkThe original donation was only the beginning of Squak Mountain State Park’s development. In March 1992, the Trust for Public Land reached an agreement with the Grand Ridge Partnership to halt a proposed housing development beside the Bullitt property. The organisation purchased 17 building lots and secured an option on another 14, with the aim of transferring the land to the state. The acquisition was completed on 18 September 1995. Another expansion occurred through Washington’s Trust Land Transfer Program, authorised in 1989. The programme allows state trust land with significant ecological or social value but limited revenue potential to be transferred into public management. It also provides a mechanism for securing replacement land that can generate income for the relevant trust beneficiaries.Through this programme, 364 acres were added to Squak Mountain State Park in 1993 and 1994, according to Washington State Parks. Other acquisitions followed, bringing together land protected through the Bullitt family’s donation and later conservation efforts. Squak Mountain State Park therefore grew through a combination of private generosity, public investment and sustained local advocacy. The siblings’ 1972 gift established the original wilderness area; subsequent purchases and volunteer efforts helped protect a much larger landscape for future generations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Centre orders probe into student suicide at IIIT Ranchi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Amid allegations of delayed medical assistance following the death of a first-year student at IIIT Ranchi, the education ministry Tuesday
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Amid allegations of delayed medical assistance following the death of a first-year student at IIIT Ranchi, the education ministry Tuesday constituted a three-member committee to examine the circ-umstances surrounding the incident and possible gaps in the institute's student support and emergency response systems.The decision comes amid protests by students, who have accused the administration of failing to provide timely medical assistance and demanded the resignation of institute director Rajiv Srivastava.The student, Aditya Kumar (20), was found hanging in his hostel room Saturday.The committee, headed by Delhi University South Campus director Rajni Abbi, will include a senior psychiatrist and a senior education ministry official. The panel will examine whether the institute has adequately implemented guidelines concerning institutional support, counselling, mentoring and student grievance redress mechanisms.It will also interact with stakeholders, examine institutional records and identify systemic gaps, besides recommending measures to strengthen student welfare and prevent similar incidents. The ministry said it was also undertaking interim administrative arrangements to ensure smooth functioning of the institute.The ministry has not specified a deadline for the committee to submit its findings. The allegations of negligence remain under examination.IIIT Ranchi operates under a public-private partnership model.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Ensure terror does not find haven: Amit Shah at Bimstec meet
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Home minister Amit Shah Tuesday said the shared resolve of Bimstec nations - Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Home minister Amit Shah Tuesday said the shared resolve of Bimstec nations - Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand - should be to ensure terrorist networks are not allowed to find safe havens, recruit members, provide training, raise terror funds or carry out activities against neighbouring countries from any part of the Bay of Bengal region.Addressing the first Bimstec home ministers' conference - which concluded in Delhi with the adoption of the Delhi Declaration that reaffirms shared commitment of member countries to strengthening regional security, trust and cooperation in the Bay of Bengal region by responding to shared challenges such as terrorism, violent extremism, drug-trafficking, organised crime, cybercrimes, money laundering, terror financing and smuggling of arms "in the spirit of cooperation and shared responsibility" - Shah said Bimstec is not just a regional organisation but "has become an essential platform for regional integration, economic cooperation and collective security".Shah listed five key areas of cooperation - drug control, counter-terrorism and legal cooperation, repatriation of fugitives, cybersecurity, and institutional cooperation and capacity building. Equating drug trafficking with death trafficking, he stressed the need to adopt a "whole of region" approach to fight the menace. Also recalling the proposal of PM Modi to establish a Bimstec disaster management centre in India, he said it will be coming up in Jamnagar, Gujarat, underscoring India's role as a 'first responder' in disaster management across the region.The meeting approved the Bimstec convention against trafficking, Bimstec plan of action on drug control and an MoU on capacity building to combat money-laundering.With scam compounds in South East Asia not only committing trans-national cyber frauds but also forcing trafficked victims from other countries to commit cybercrime from their premises, the declaration stressed the urgency of cooperation among the states of origin, transit and destination of victims.The declaration also condemned terrorism, including cross-border terrorism, with Bimstec nations reiterating their resolve to prevent and eliminate these threats in a comprehensive manner. The home ministers expressed deepest condolences and solidarity with the victims of terrorism attacks in member states and their families, as well as with govt of the affected states, and called for the perpetrators to be brought to justice.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a phone conversation on Tuesday, PM Modi and his Canadian counterpart, Mark Carney, reaffirmed their commitment to finalising the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement at the earliest and doubling bilateral trade by 2030. Modi will visit Canada in Dec - on his way to the G20 summit in US - and the trade agreement is expected during the trip.India is also discussing a possible visit by Carney in Jan as chief guest for Republic Day. Canada foreign minister Anita Anand and trade minister Maninder Sidhu are visiting India currently.Modi said the two agreed to build on the positive momentum in ties and work for concrete outcomes across key areas, including trade, energy, tech security and people-to-people ties. "Had a warm and productive conversation with PM Mark Carney. Together, India and Canada are contributing towards a more stable and prosperous world," Modi tweeted. tnnModi & Carney welcome increased India-Canada engagement over last year According to a Canadian readout, the PMs welcomed the increased engagement between Canada and India over the past year, including in areas such as finance, defence and security, people-to-people ties and artificial intelligence. They underscored the opportunity to build on this renewed momentum."The leaders also discussed the impact of geopolitical instability in the Indo-Pacific region and the need for trusted partners in the areas of energy and agriculture," said the Canadian readout, adding that Carney thanked Modi for his leadership in seeking a peaceful resolution to Russia's war on Ukraine.The leaders welcomed the bilateral security dialogue that took place in India last week as part of the ongoing security and law enforcement engagement at the national security adviser level. They also agreed to remain in close contact ahead of Modi's visit to Canada in Dec."They welcomed the historic Team Canada Trade Mission currently taking place in India, led by the minister of international trade, Maninder Sidhu, as well as a visit to New Delhi this week by the minister of foreign affairs, Anita Anand, to advance shared priorities, including trade, energy and people-to-people ties," read the readout.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
articles.summary: The Ukrainian president says the ballistic missile strikes came with "no early warning from our partners".
articles.body:
A key energy facility supplying Kyiv with heating and electricity has been hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

Darnytska CHP-4, or CHPP-4, and a residential building were hit in a strike the president said came with "no early warning from our partners".

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said one person was killed and 13 injured in the missile strike on the apartment block late on Tuesday. Four people were in a serious condition, he said.

It comes two days after US President Donald Trump said an energy ceasefire had been agreed by Russia and Ukraine, although Kyiv reported multiple Russian strikes following the announcement.

"Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people," Zelensky said on social media following Tuesday's strikes.

"This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added.

"It is important that the world does not stay silent about this. And it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing."

It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles.

Following strikes on Monday night, there was speculation America had cut off access to key intelligence enabling Ukraine to track incoming threats.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump denied that was the case.

"We are helping them and we are sharing intel," he said.

"We want the war to end. So we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end."

Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites, Trump said: "Ukraine hit many sites the day before."

But he demurred when asked if Russia had broken a ceasefire. He said both countries want the war to "come to an end" but "just don't know how to get there".

It comes after Zelensky said on Sunday that a 60-day ceasefire would allow ⁠his country to hold presidential elections, following comments from Trump that "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".

Following Trump's announcement on Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Ukraine doesn't deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

Lavrov added that under any ceasefire, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war.

CHPP-4, which provides heating and electricity to the Dniprovskyi district and parts of the Darnytskyi district, has been hit multiple times during the war.

It was severely damaged in a separate Russian missile attack in February this year, which forced it to shut down.

That strike left more than 1,000 residential buildings without heating and hot water, along with 47 schools, 72 kindergartens and 18 medical institutions, according to Reuters.

articles.title: In 2008, Michael Phelps used his $1 million Olympic bonus to start a foundation; by 2020, its programmes had reached more than 100,000 young people
articles.summary: Winning eight gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics brought Michael Phelps worldwide recognition, but the swimmer also wanted to use his success to
articles.body: Winning eight gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics brought Michael Phelps worldwide recognition, but the swimmer also wanted to use his success to make a difference beyond the pool. He put his $1 million sponsor bonus towards establishing the Michael Phelps Foundation, an initiative focused on encouraging swimming, water safety and healthy living among young people. According to Boys & Girls Clubs of America, one of the foundation’s early efforts was a nationwide tour promoting his “Dream, Plan, Reach” message. Over the following years, its programmes expanded to include mental health education, reaching children through partnerships with youth organisations.From Olympic success to a wider purposePhelps had already made history in Beijing in 2008, winning eight gold medals at a single Olympic Games. But rather than keeping the entire sponsor bonus for himself, he used the $1 million to establish a foundation that could help more children discover swimming and learn skills that extend beyond sport. The Michael Phelps Foundation was established that year with a focus on water safety, youth swimming, wellness and goal-setting. Its early “Dream, Plan, Reach” initiative encouraged children to set ambitions and work towards them through consistent effort. The message reflected a familiar part of Phelps’ own sporting journey: success requires a clear goal, planning and the determination to keep going.The foundation began working with Boys & Girls Clubs of America, a network that provides programmes and support for young people in communities across the United States. Its early nationwide tour took Phelps’ message to club members, connecting his experience as an Olympic athlete with children who might not otherwise have access to structured swimming or development programmes.A swimming programme with lessons beyond the poolOne of the foundation’s main initiatives is the “im” programme, developed with KidsHealth.org and the Michael Phelps Swim School. The name refers both to the individual medley, Phelps’ signature swimming event, and the words “I am”, reinforcing the idea of self-belief and personal growth. The programme combines swimming instruction and water-safety education with healthy living and goal-setting. Rather than concentrating only on athletic performance, it aims to help children become more comfortable in the water while developing confidence and habits that can support them in everyday life.According to Boys & Girls Clubs of America, the programme launched in 2010 at six clubs and expanded to 28 clubs by 2012. The foundation supports participating clubs through financial assistance, training, staff support, equipment, pool access and learning materials. These resources help organisations deliver lessons to children who may face barriers to swimming opportunities.Water safety is an important part of the initiative. Learning to swim can give children practical skills around pools and other bodies of water, while structured lessons can help them become more confident. The programme also uses goal-setting to encourage participants to recognise progress, work towards achievable targets and develop a sense of accomplishment.Expanding the mission to mental healthThe foundation’s work later grew to include children’s emotional wellbeing. Its partnership with Nemours Children’s Health helped bring mental health education into its programmes, recognising that young people need support with emotional challenges as well as physical health and safety. During the COVID-19 pandemic, this aspect of the work became especially relevant. School closures, separation from friends and changes to familiar routines created difficulties for many children. In October 2021, Nemours Children’s Health and the Michael Phelps Foundation announced that their “IM Healthy” social-emotional learning programme had reached more than 50,000 children through 174 Boys & Girls Clubs of America.The programme drew on research and practices from areas including child development, psychology and paediatrics. Its lessons were designed to help children understand emotions, develop coping skills and recognise that it is normal not to feel okay all the time. The initiative extended the foundation’s original focus on healthy living by addressing the connection between emotional and physical wellbeing. The partnership also reflected Phelps’ growing willingness to speak publicly about mental health. By supporting conversations about emotions and resilience, the foundation sought to make such topics easier for children to discuss in supportive settings.Reaching children through partnershipsThe foundation’s reach has depended on working with organisations that already serve young people. Through Boys & Girls Clubs of America, Special Olympics International and other partners, its programmes have reached children and young people in different communities.A 2020 announcement reported that the foundation had provided learn-to-swim, healthy living and goal-setting programmes to more than 100,000 children and young adults around the world. The 2021 announcement from Nemours recorded a separate milestone for the “IM Healthy” curriculum, which reached more than 50,000 children through 174 Boys & Girls Clubs of America. These figures reflect different programme measures rather than a single cumulative total. Together, they illustrate how the foundation’s work expanded from swimming and goal-setting into emotional wellbeing education.A legacy beyond medalsPhelps’ Olympic achievements remain central to his public identity, but the foundation represents another part of his legacy. The $1 million bonus that followed his record-setting performance in Beijing helped establish a programme focused on skills children can use long after a swimming lesson ends.By combining water safety, healthy living, goal-setting and mental health education, the Michael Phelps Foundation has broadened its mission beyond sport. Its work shows how an athlete’s success can support initiatives that help young people develop confidence, resilience and safer, healthier habits.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'Whistle-blower' CRPF officer seeks probe into 'mistreatment' of protesters
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A serving CRPF officer posted in Manipur has approached National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), National Commission for Women (NCW) and Delhi
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A serving CRPF officer posted in Manipur has approached National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), National Commission for Women (NCW) and Delhi Police commissioner, seeking an impartial enquiry into three videos circulated on social media, where certain CAPF and police personnel appear to be "physically mistreating" women protesting against SIR and CEC Gyanesh Kumar in Delhi.CRPF assistant commandant Rahul Solanki, who has a history of playing vigilante and whistle-blower, having alleged poor living conditions of CRPF personnel deployed in Jharkhand for 2019 assembly poll and more recently claiming "unauthorised sale" of track suits at CRPF group centre in Greater Noida, clarified in his letter that he was submitting the complaint "in my individual capacity as a concerned citizen of India, committed to the rule of law, and the dignity and safety of women".Sharing three video links that form the basis of his complaint dated Oct 11, he requested an impartial probe and forensic verification of the incident and the circumstances. He added a disclaimer, saying the videos were obtained by him strictly for verification purposes and had not been authenticated. Solanki insisted that he was not endorsing the views and statements of any individuals or organisations behind the videos.Seeking any genuine misconduct on part of the police/CAPF personnel to be addressed fairly, he said in case the allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women protesters are substantiated, appropriate legal and departmental action may follow against the personnel and their supervisors. Alternatively, if the footage is found to be fabricated or manipulated, legal action and removal of the misleading content, should be pursued as per law. He also requested gender sensitivity training for police personnel on the ground.A CRPF official told TOI that Solanki's act of directly approaching the rights watchdogs and Delhi Police against the conduct of CAPF/police officers, rather than raise the matter with his superiors, may be viewed as indiscipline as service conduct rules bar officers from filing public complaints against govt officers/depts. "The officer concerned was not even on the ground (where protests were held). If he was concerned, he would have raised the matter internally with his superiors," said an officer. The officer hinted that Solanki could face departmental proceedings over violation of conduct rules.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2023, a Los Angeles man paid $50 for an old leather chair on Facebook Marketplace; months later, experts identified the rare 1930s design, and it sold for $107,950
articles.summary: Justin Miller, a home design content creator from Los Angeles, spent half an hour scrolling through Facebook Marketplace.
articles.body: Justin Miller, a home design content creator from Los Angeles, spent half an hour scrolling through Facebook Marketplace. Most days, the search turned up nothing worth a second look. But in February 2023, he stumbled upon something unique: a chair. And that chair changed his year. He bought it for $50 and ended up selling it at a Sotheby’s auction on June 7 for $107,950 (including premiums).An unassuming chairThe listing was part of a yard sale at a home in Beverly Hills. The seller wanted $50 for a leather armchair. Miller, who was only 33 at the time, thought the colour of the leather was striking. He also liked the shape, which looked unusual to him. Although he knew little about furniture, he thought the chair was a bargain. “I’m not a furniture expert by any means. But I have a good eye, and I can tell when something is really unique,” Miller said in a TikTok post after finding the chair. That was enough for him to pay the asking price and drive the chair home.While he was arranging a collection time with the seller, he received a message that stuck with him. The seller told him that if he repaired the chair, it would be worth a lot. Miller took the comment seriously. He searched online and learned that the chair was truly unique.The oak and leather chair was made by Frits Henningsen, a Danish designer who worked in the 1930s. Only about 50 of these chairs were believed to have been made. Some similar pieces had already sold for six figures.Reaching out to Sotheby’sMiller posted about his find on social media, and the comments were full of advice. Many viewers told him to contact an auction house, and he did. He reached out to Sotheby’s, and they agreed to restore the chair and sell it. They repaired the torn areas, conditioned the leather and tightened the fabric under the seat. The auction house gave the chair a pre-sale estimate of $30,000 to $50,000.Three minutes and a number that simply didn’t make senseThe auction on June 7 lasted just under three minutes. Bids climbed past the estimate, and the chair sold for $85,000. With the buyer’s premium, the final total came to $107,950.Miller watched the sale live and recorded his reaction. The video went viral, garnering over four million views in a matter of hours. Carina Villinger, Sotheby’s head of 20th-century design, said the result set a record price for a chair by Henningsen. “We are absolutely delighted that Justin’s chair achieved this outstanding result. From the moment he contacted Sotheby’s to restore and sell his armchair, we’ve enjoyed learning about his discovery, which achieved a record price for this model by Frits Henningsen,” she told TODAY.Miller is delighted that his $50 chair earned him a fortune. He continues to hunt for bargains. “People always tell me they don’t find anything good on Facebook Marketplace. But they just aren’t looking hard enough.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Generate questions at last minute to prevent paper leaks: Nilekani
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Question papers for high-stakes entrance examinations could be generated at the last minute from a massive bank of questions instead of being
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Question papers for high-stakes entrance examinations could be generated at the last minute from a massive bank of questions instead of being prepared and stored in advance, as part of a technology-driven overhaul to prevent leaks, Nandan Nilekani, chairperson of the high-powered task force on examination reforms, said on Tuesday. He also said PM Modi was keen to implement the panel's recommendations.Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 in Delhi, the Infosys chairperson questioned the need for a fixed question paper, arguing that its existence created an economic incentive for theft and sale."Why do we need to have something called a question paper? Because the moment you have a question paper, that creates an economic incentive for that to be sold," Nilekani said. He suggested creating a massive question bank from which the paper would be assembled just before the examination. This, he said, would eliminate the incentive for advance leaks.Nilekani: Need to expand comp-based testing infrastructureAsked whether artificial intelligence could generate papers on examination day, Nandan Nilekani, replied, "Yeah, sure." The proposal comes as the six-member task force prepares to submit its report later this month, following extensive consultations on examination security, technology and governance.TOI reported on Oct 1 that the panel was prioritising "debundling" examination responsibilities by separating question-paper setting, exam conduct, test-centre management and security among different agencies. The restructuring seeks to reduce concentration of control over exams. A common calendar for major recruitment and entrance tests is also under consideration.Earlier, on Sept 16, TOI reported that multiple attempts at high-stakes entrance examinations and better-equipped, secure testing centres were among the prominent suggestions received by the task force. The recommendations included reliable electricity, internet connectivity, biometric verification and CCTV surveillance.He also stressed expanding computer-based testing infrastructure. He said the existing network of around 1.5 lakh testing locations needed to grow to accommodate a wider shift towards computer-based examinations."If you look at it systematically and go to root causes of why it's happening and use technology to solve it... they are solvable issues," he said.Constituted on July 26 following the NEET-UG controversy and the student protests, the task force has held around 18 panel meetings and 40 consultations. It has received over 50,000 suggestions from students, parents, professional associations and examination bodies.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Actress Selma Blair faces additional charges for assault after plane incident
articles.summary: The Legally Blonde actress faces two counts of assault for allegedly kicking a police officer and a nurse after allegedly attacking attendants on a flight.
articles.body:
US actress Selma Blair has been charged with two additional assault counts over allegedly kicking an officer and a nurse after being removed from a flight.

Blair was arrested late Sunday in New York after she allegedly attacked flight attendants on a Delta plane travelling from Los Angeles to New York. The FBI issued her a federal summons accusing her of assault on board.

While appearing in court over the additional charges, the Legally Blonde star's attorney asked the judge to consider the actress's "body of work", and called Blair the "gold standard." The judge said she should not "get special treatment".

Blair has pleaded not guilty. She has since been released on bail.

She was taken to hospital after the incident on the flight. Her representatives have told the BBC that she had "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct".

As the flight landed in New York on Sunday evening, airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.

Audio recorded on air traffic control details a pilot asking for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner.

Blair, 54, who also starred in Cruel Intentions and Hellboy, was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US.

The two additional charges of assault, filed in state court, came after she was taken off the plane.

One of the alleged assaults happened when she was being transported in an ambulance, where she allegedly kicked a police officer. Once at hospital, prosecutors allege that she also assaulted a nurse.

At her arraignment in Queens, Blair's attorney Shawn Barnes asked the judge for leniency. He said that "violence" is "not who she is" and asked for the judge to consider her body of work.

The actress is somebody that people she look up to, he said, referring to her as "the gold standard".

The judge denied his request and said she "should not get special treatment...because she is a celebrity".

The judge set her bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond with the next hearing scheduled for 19 January. It is unclear when a date will be set for the federal case against her, which concerns the allegations of assault aboard the aircraft.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI/MUMBAI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman Tuesday said the govt was open and keen to \"hear\" discussions around the long-term capital gains
articles.body: NEW DELHI/MUMBAI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman Tuesday said the govt was open and keen to "hear" discussions around the long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax as it was "healthy" to have the debate.The minister, however, declined to be specific on the matter as preparations for the Union Budget in Feb are already underway.The FM's comments raised investors' hopes of a reduction in LTCG tax and securities transaction tax (STT), a longstanding demand among foreign funds who have been big sellers in the Indian market in the last two years.As a result, after a steady start, stock prices jumped with the sensex finally settling 1.5% or 1,109 points up at 73,034 points while Nifty closed 1.6% or 359 points up at 22,722 points.RBI steps to check rupee volatility: FM While responding to an observation that investors, especially foreign funds, were keen on removal of capital gains tax and streamlining of taxation before they started investing in India, Sitharaman said, "Two years ago, we had bought all the asset classes similarly and people thought that I was increasing the tax. I was not increasing the tax, I was bringing all of them at par, so that an investor is not speculating as to which one gives them greater leverage. So, these are the things on which there is a lot of debate. It's healthy to have this debate and I will be keen to hear them."At a Bloomberg event, FM acknowledged that investors, both within and outside, were commenting on LTCG and the question of treating all asset classes similarly has been a widely discussed topic.So far this year, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have bet sold Indian stocks worth a little over Rs 3 lakh crore, NSDL data showed. In 2025, the corresponding figure was a net outflow of nearly Rs 1.7 lakh crore and just Rs 427 crore in 2024. Since Sept 2024, sensex has lost about 13%.At the same event, Sitharaman also noted that rupee has depreciated "significantly" over the past year and a half, and RBI will continue its efforts to prevent excessive volatility. "RBI is not trying to fix the rupee, it is trying to stop the volatility, and for that there is a lot of effort from their side. I am sure RBI will take further steps to make sure that rupee does not become too volatile," she said in response to a query on capital outflows, especially in the equity market due to currency depreciation.FM stressed that govt has kept the economy on a sound footing and been careful with its spending and borrowings, helping investors looking to diversify away from China. "Fiscal discipline is not going to be a matter which should worry investors," she said, adding that domestic private capital is moving in and is attracting private capital from elsewhere as well.At a time when foreign funds are taking money out of India at a fast clip, a relook at the taxes related to the markets is a welcome move.According to Hitesh Sawhney, partner at Price Waterhouse, against the current backdrop of sustained foreign investor selling, elevated global yields and capital moving towards competing markets, revisiting LTCG taxation may be timely."A (zero) tax rate on LTCG, linked to a relatively longer holding period, could reward patient capital, encourage investors to remain invested in India and strengthen India's relative capital market attractiveness. It would also reduce foreign investors' dependence on treaty-based exemptions and the resulting uncertainty over treaty eligibility."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
articles.summary: Four years after the attacks, Serhii K will appear in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany.
articles.body:
Four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history, a Ukrainian man goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany.

Serhii K, as he is identified by German prosecutors, is accused of plotting with other Ukrainian military personnel to destroy the pipelines and stop Russia financing its war with gas revenue.

The case is highly sensitive in Germany, seen as one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.

Serhii K, extradited to Germany last year, will become the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts.

He denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.

In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.

Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.

As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.

Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock.

They said later that "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".

Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".

They say the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime" as an attack by military means against civilian objects".

Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine

The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.

Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".

He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."

However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.

"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.

In August 2025, Serhii K was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.

After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, Serhii K - identified in court documents as Serhii Kuznetsov - was transferred to Germany late last year.

German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army , and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.

While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.

In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".

Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.

Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.

Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

articles.title: Omar, Mehbooba, Mirwaiz oppose bid to enforce uniform Friday sermons
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: The J&K Waqf Board’s move to introduce uniform Friday sermons across Jammu & Kashmir has drawn fierce criticism in the region from key political
articles.body: SRINAGAR: The J&K Waqf Board’s move to introduce uniform Friday sermons across Jammu & Kashmir has drawn fierce criticism in the region from key political figures, including CM Omar Abdullah.“This is an unacceptable attempt by BJP to interfere in the religious affairs of Muslims and will not be accepted under any circumstances. The BJP-appointed chairperson must immediately halt this misplaced attempt to please her masters,” Omar said.Waqf Board chairperson Dr Darakhshan Andrabi belongs to BJP.PDP president Mehbooba Mufti called for the transfer of Waqf administration in J&K to the elected government. “This is the BJP’s agenda to harass Muslims. They want to interfere in our religious affairs. Just like the Uniform Civil Code, they also want to impose uniformity in this matter. These are our mosques, built with our people’s money. Our imams and maulvis know what to say and when,” she said.On Saturday, Andrabi chaired a meeting of muftis, imams and other religious scholars proposing a committee to identify and finalise topics for Friday sermons in advance and communicate them to mosque imams associated with Waqf-managed institutions across J&K and other mosques. The meeting, according to Andrabi, was attended by around 1,500 imams and Islamic scholars.Andrabi said the Waqf Board has not issued any order or directive on the issue.She said religious scholars and imams proposed uniform Friday sermons to address social evils like drug abuse, suicide and late marriages. “All imams and preachers had assembled and there was no role of the Waqf board officials in it,” she said.Rejecting criticism from political figures, Andrabi said Muslim scholars associated with the Waqf Board were qualified to take such decisions and urged politicians to stay out of the matter. “If politicians are of the view that imams should not talk about drug abuse and other evils, then fine,” she said.Hurriyat Conference chairman Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, who also heads Muttahida Majlis-e-Ulema (MMU), the largest representative organization of Islamic scholars, imams, and socio-religious bodies in J&K, said MMU strongly rejects any attempt by the Waqf Board to prescribe uniform Friday sermons. “The religious guidance is the domain of ulema and imams, not state-linked bodies. Such interference in matters of faith and religious practice is unacceptable. The Waqf Board must confine itself to its administrative responsibilities,” Mirwaiz said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: General:Fortune has a generous mood toward you today. Keep a simple schedule and finish one subject at a time. articles.title: DAY 4 KUSHMANDA: Creation Begins Before the Light
articles.summary: For nearly 380,000 years after the beginning of the universe, light could not travel freely.
articles.body: For nearly 380,000 years after the beginning of the universe, light could not travel freely. The cosmos was a hot, dense plasma in which photons repeatedly collided with charged particles. Only when the universe cooled enough for atoms to form did it become transparent, releasing an ancient glow that still surrounds us.Creation had begun long before light could be seen.This is a beautiful doorway into Kushmanda, the Mother of the cosmic egg. She is remembered as the gentle radiance that awakens a sleeping universe. Her smile suggests that creation is not born only through force. It also emerges through warmth, spaciousness and delight.The scriptures and cosmology speak different languages, yet both remind us that beginnings are often hidden. Darkness need not mean emptiness. It may be a womb in which form is still learning how to appear.The Rigveda opens not with a theory but with Agni, the living flame: priest, invoker and bearer of the offering. Fire makes relationship possible. It receives what human hands can offer and carries it towards what the heart reveres.In the Devi Sukta, the Mother declares that her womb lies within the cosmic waters and that she gives birth to the Father at the summit. The source of creation is presented not as a distant object but as a living presence from which even the powers that order existence arise.The Durga Saptashati offers another luminous image. The separate radiances of the devas converge and assume the form of the Goddess. What was scattered becomes one purposeful brilliance. Light here is not display; it is awakened capacity.Vision physiology adds a further wonder. Light itself is not yet sight. A photon must enter the eye and be captured by light-sensitive proteins in the rods or cones. That encounter becomes an electrical signal, carried to the brain and shaped into the image we experience. Under carefully controlled conditions, human observers can detect even a single photon above chance.The lesson is quietly astonishing: illumination requires both radiance and receptivity. A thousand lamps cannot make a closed eye see, while the faintest light may matter to an eye prepared to receive it.On the fourth day, sit before a small flame and ask two questions. What is trying to be born through me? What must become receptive for that birth to occur? An idea, a reconciliation, a page of writing or an act of service may still be passing through its unseen beginning. Do not drag it prematurely into the glare of judgement. Give it warmth, discipline and time.Creation begins before light becomes visible. Vision begins before an image enters awareness. Grace begins before transformation can be named.Kushmanda’s smile tells us that darkness may already be carrying dawn. One true flame is enough, not because it illuminates the whole universe, but because it gives the darkness a direction.Authored by: Dr Shambo Samrat Samajdar and Dr Shashank R Joshi

articles.title: In 1998, Jeremy Irons bought a ruined 15th-century Irish castle and spent over five years restoring it; he later bought a tiny island beside it
articles.summary: British actor Jeremy Irons bought the historic Kilcoe Castle in County Cork, Ireland, in 1998 with his wife, actress Sinéad Cusack, and spent years
articles.body: British actor Jeremy Irons bought the historic Kilcoe Castle in County Cork, Ireland, in 1998 with his wife, actress Sinéad Cusack, and spent years restoring the medieval property. The castle was later joined by another acquisition: a small island nearby, with a cottage. In January 2022, Irons revealed the purchase during an appearance on Late Night with Seth Meyers, explaining that the island was around 100 metres from the castle. He also said he plans to keep Kerry ponies and Galloway cattle there, adding that he spends more time farming than acting.How did Jeremy Irons restore Kilcoe CastleIrons bought Kilcoe Castle in 1998 with Cusack. Located in south County Cork, the medieval structure became the focus of an extensive restoration project. According to Raidió Teilifís Éireann, Ireland's national public service media broadcaster, the castle was refurbished over five years, while the actor worked on the property.The restoration involved rebuilding the castle's castellations, the defensive features along the top of its walls. Irons explained in a television interview that the work was carefully planned, with models prepared before construction began. However, once the castellations were completed, he realised that the finished structure was smaller than he had intended.How Jeremy Irons corrected a mistake during Castle’s restorationIrons recounted how he decided to inspect the newly built castellations himself after noticing the problem. One of his friends suggested that he speak directly to the builders rather than leaving the matter to someone else. The actor then climbed 13 floors of scaffolding to reach the top of the castle.In an interview with Raidió Teilifís Éireann, describing the conversation with the workers, Irons said: “This is wonderful, guys, this is wonderful what you've built, but actually you got to take it down; we've got to make it bigger. It's not strong enough.” RTÉ reported that the exchange ended with one of the builders remarking on the difficulties of working with actors, saying, “The trouble with working with bloody actors is the bloody rehearsals.”Why did Jeremy Irons buy a tiny island near Kilcoe CastleIn his January 2022 appearance on Late Night with Seth Meyers, Irons disclosed that he had acquired a small island close to Kilcoe Castle. He described its proximity to the castle by explaining that it was approximately 100 metres away and that he could almost swim between the two properties. The island also has a small cottage, according to the actor's description during the interview. He commented on the additional property, which he said he intended to use for agricultural purposes. His remarks followed the television appearance.Irons said he intended to rear Kerry ponies and Galloway cattle on the island. Explaining the purpose of keeping the animals there, he said they would help “eat it down”, referring to managing the vegetation through grazing.Speaking about his activities, Irons added: “I'm farming a little bit more than I'm acting.” His remarks indicated that farming had become a significant part of his routine alongside his work in film and television.Why Irons supports reopening Dublin’s historic Iveagh MarketsAlongside Kilcoe Castle and the island near it, Irons owns a house in the Liberties area of Dublin. RTÉ reported that he had spoken in November 2021 about his support for a local campaign seeking to reopen the long-abandoned Iveagh Markets.The campaign aims to bring the historic market building back into use as a resource for the surrounding community. Irons expressed support for the initiative during an interview with RTÉ Entertainment conducted while he was promoting House of Gucci. The film featured Irons as Rodolfo Gucci, while he also appeared in Munich: The Edge of War as British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain. His time in Ireland and his comments about farming reflect activities beyond his acting career.
